items.title: Harold Mabern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, March 31, 2010
items.q: I’ve always been attracted to chords. I love chords you know. Plus I did a lot of listening to George Shearing who is one of my heroes. That’s why I said harmonically speaking you know the people talk about Bill Evans but I’ve always been more involved with George Shearing’s harmonic gestures, you k

ctx.x: But you had this interest in bebop, and where did that come from at that age? Was it by the radio or buying LPs?

No, see that’s the thing. On the radio you didn’t hear no — first of all, on the radio you would hear maybe some Dave Brubeck and some George Shearing, but you didn’t really hear no Art Tatum, Charlie Parker, Bud Powell, at that time because that was too strong © Fillius Jazz Archive -3-

for the airways. So even then, the artists who played that way had to play in a more commercial-type vein. But we always had big bands that would come to Memphis, like the Count Basie big band, or the Duke Ellington big band, or the Lionel Hampton Orchestra and they would play it at the Palace Theater and on that group would be like a big band, a jazz vocalist, maybe Sarah Vaughan or Ella Fitzgerald or something like that, and a comedian, and that would be it.
